what: The two AI plans of the final evaluation's live FX run (1 Oct 2026), verbatim: the page's /plan response bodies' `plan` (.work/eval/out/final-2026-10-01/quant-fx/requests/01_plan-response.json and 02_plan-response.json; the second is the re-plan after the engine's signals, and the plan the report ran). The file they read is the StatCan 33-10-0036-01 U.S. dollar series (tools/fixtures/eval/fx_usd_cad.csv, rebuilt to the published 15 columns by tools/test_nl_browser.py _fx_published). Public data (Statistics Canada Open Licence); no personal data.

plan_1.goal: How has the Canadian dollar moved against the US dollar since 2017, and what should a Canadian importer expect next?
goal_candidates: Where does the latest CAD/USD rate sit against its 2017–2026 average, and how wide has its trading band been?
How differently did the loonie behave in 2017–2019, 2020–2021 and 2022–2026, and which stretch moved fastest?
What does the month-by-year pattern of the CAD/USD rate say about seasonality?
How did the CAD/USD rate react around the 2020 pandemic shock and the 2022 rate-hike cycle?
What 12-month range should a Canadian importer budget for, based on the full 2017–2026 distribution of the rate?
How reliable is a time-based forecast of the CAD/USD rate when tested on held-out recent dates?
plan_1.understanding: This is Statistics Canada's daily noon exchange rate for the U.S. dollar in Canadian dollars, one row per calendar date from January 2017 to August 2026. Each row is a single day: 2,957 of the 3,526 dates carry an observed rate, while the rest are weekend and statutory-holiday non-observations recorded as 0 or left blank with STATUS '..'. VALUE is a level — Canadian dollars per one US dollar — so a rise means a weaker Canadian dollar and costlier US imports for a Canadian importer. Only one geography (Canada) and one currency pair are present, so this is a single long daily series rather than a panel.

analyses.why: The long-run direction and pace of the CAD/USD rate since 2017 — the core of the question.
How wide the rate's band is, so an importer can budget a realistic CAD-per-USD range.
A forward-looking signal for the coming months, scored on dates the model did not see.

quality_risks: 550 values are exactly 0 and 569 are blank: these are weekend/holiday non-observations, not a rate of zero — reading them as real would drag every average down.
The final month (2026-08) is likely partial, so any latest-value or recent-average figure covers fewer days than earlier months.
VALUE is CAD per 1 USD, so an increase means a weaker Canadian dollar and more expensive US goods; the direction is easy to misread as 'the dollar strengthening'.
The span covers very different regimes (2017–2019, the 2020 shock, the 2022 rate-hike cycle), so a single straight-line forecast understates how abruptly the rate can shift.
Every row is the same country and currency, so any apparent cross-entity comparison in the file would be meaningless.

charts.why: Month across by year down shows the CAD/USD regime shifts and any seasonal pattern at a glance.

goal_candidates: How wide has the CAD/USD range been since 2017, and how often has the rate sat near its weakest levels?
In which months and years has the loonie been strongest or weakest — is there a seasonal pattern an importer could time purchases around?

plan_2.understanding: A Statistics Canada / Bank of Canada daily-average exchange-rate table holding a single series: the US dollar priced in Canadian dollars from January 2017 to August 2026. Each row is one calendar day; VALUE is that day's average rate in CAD per USD (roughly 1.25-1.46). 569 rows carry no value at all (STATUS '..', weekends/holidays) and 550 values are placeholder zeros, which the engine reads as gaps because the column is a level with zeros_missing_if_level set. GEO and Type of currency are constant labels (Canada; U.S. dollar, daily average) and every other column is a fixed code with one distinct value.

columns.name: REF_DATE
columns.why: daily date stamp; the file's whole timeline

columns.name: VALUE
columns.why: the daily-average rate in Canadian dollars per US dollar — the number the question is about

columns.name: GEO
columns.why: constant label: the series is Canada

columns.name: Type of currency
columns.why: constant label: U.S. dollar, daily average (CAD per USD)

columns.name: STATUS
columns.why: marks '..' on rows where VALUE is blank; holds nothing once blanks are dropped

analyses.why: long-run pace of the loonie, by decade and over the last years the file covers
how wide the 2017-2026 range has been and where the latest rate sits inside it

quality_risks: VALUE holds 550 placeholder zeros and 569 blanks (STATUS '..'): weekend/holiday days with no rate. Typed as a level, the engine reads each 0 as a gap, so the series must never be averaged with those zeros counted as real values.
VALUE is Canadian dollars per US dollar, a daily-average reference rate: a rise means the loonie weakens. An importer reading a rising line as 'the dollar going up' will get the direction backwards.
The coverage ends in August 2026, so the final year is partial (eight months) and its averages and changes are not comparable with full calendar years.
This is one daily-average reference rate with no bid/ask spread or bank fees, so an importer's actual conversion cost sits above it.

All remaining columns (UOM, UOM_ID, SCALAR_FACTOR, SCALAR_ID, COORDINATE, DECIMALS) are constants with a single distinct value and carry no signal — using any of them as a driver would produce meaningless output.

charts.why: month across, year down: shows the seasonal swings and the drift in the rate an importer can plan purchases around
